items.title: This part is about a URL decoder, the small function that turns a percent sign and two characters into the character they stand for, and about how one malformed request can leave a Node server unable to answer anybody for 20 seconds.

claims.line: This part is about a URL decoder, the small function that turns a percent sign and two characters into the character they stand for, and about how one malformed request can leave a Node server unable to answer anybody for 20 seconds.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: A decoder having a bad twenty seconds. That is the least dramatic outage I have ever been sold.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: It is the most common one, though. Picture a form on a small service you run yourself. Somebody posts a body full of percent-encoded junk. Not a flood. One request. The decoder walks the whole string, and while it walks it, nothing else in that process happens. Everybody else waiting on that server is waiting behind that one request.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: And nothing gets stolen.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Nothing stolen, nothing changed. The advisory says it plainly: availability only, no confidentiality or integrity impact. Which is the sentence that makes people stop reading, right up until the thing that is unavailable is the only copy of the service they have.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Fine. What is actually slow?
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: The fallback. There are two decoders in this package. The fast one is built into the language, and it refuses input it does not like. When it refuses, the package falls back to a hand-written one, and that one has a shape problem.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Shape.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: It scans the input for every distinct run of percent-encoded bytes and writes each one into a lookup table. Then, for every entry in that table, it does one search and replace across the entire string. So the work is the number of distinct escapes multiplied by the length of the string.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: And the attacker picks both of those numbers.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Both. Thirty-two thousand distinct escapes inside a couple of hundred kilobytes, and you have thirty-two thousand sweeps of the same string. That is where the twenty seconds goes.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Why is there a fallback at all?
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Because real input is malformed and the native decoder throws. The slow path exists for bad input. So the path an attacker needs is the path you wrote for exactly this situation, and one bad sequence at the end of a payload is enough to send you down it.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: You do not have to beat the fast decoder. You make it give up.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Here is the mistake, and it is one I would make. You hear URL decoder, you think URLs, and you think about the header limit: 16 kilobytes for a request header, so a query string can only get so bad. And that part is true. Through a query string the worst case lands around 40 milliseconds. Annoying. Not fatal.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Then somebody reads the body.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Somebody reads the body. The payload that costs 20 seconds is 224 kilobytes, which is not a large thing to send, and there is no header limit between you and it. If your form parsing hands the body to this same function, the advisory names a common query-string parser as one of the routes in, then the limit you were counting on sits on the wrong side of the request.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: So who is exposed?
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: You are, if untrusted input reaches this function, whether you call it or a dependency calls it on your behalf. You are not, if the only strings you decode are ones you produced yourself. And there is a sting for anybody who has been keeping up: the release that fixed the previous bug in this package is one of the affected versions. The last fix replaced one routine and left this replacement loop exactly as it was.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: So the version people moved to for safety is the version with the hole in it.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: That is the part worth keeping. A fix answers the bug it was written for. It does not audit the shape of the code around it, and quadratic work is invisible in review, because every line in that loop looks cheap. One scan is cheap. Two scans is cheap. Thirty-two thousand scans of the same string is an outage.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: And the fix tonight?
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: The patched release. Nothing in the advisory offers you a clever setting instead. The cost is a dependency bump you did not schedule, in a package you probably did not choose, which something else installed for you. So the job is not the upgrade itself. The job is finding out whether it is in your tree at all.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: Which is the least satisfying answer in security. Patch a thing you have never heard of, in a place you cannot see. That one is still unverified.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: This is the bit where I say on your own metal, and tonight I mean it twice. On your own metal there is one process and one thread. Nothing spins up behind you because a graph went vertical, so twenty seconds is twenty seconds for every single person on that box.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: In the cloud it would be twenty seconds and an invoice for the instances that failed to help. That one is still unverified.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: That is the cloud conspiracy and you said it for me. But it cuts both ways: the same box that has nobody to save it is the box where you can see exactly which request did the damage. That one is still unverified.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: So the advice is patch, and the consolation is that you will know who did it. That one is still unverified.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

claims.line: The advice is patch, and the lesson is bigger than the package. When a function gets slower as the input grows, the attacker gets to choose the input. That is true of this decoder tonight, and it will be true of something else next month.
claims.title: GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

items.title: Have you ever opened a chat on your phone, then tried to edit it on your desktop, only to find the history is totally different?

claims.line: Have you ever opened a chat on your phone, then tried to edit it on your desktop, only to find the history is totally different?
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: This release fixes that by ensuring one gateway owns every conversation, so the CLI, TUI, and Desktop all attach to the same queue.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: In other words, it’s one brain for all the faces.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Exactly. And you can now serve that whole Desktop workspace from your own gateway in a browser tab, off by default until you toggle the setting.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Well, actually, you need to enable it in Settings or via the flag, but yes, it ships in the Docker image and the Nix package.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: So I can access it from anywhere on my network?
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Yes, behind a public URL with sign-in if you want, but locally it’s just a tab in your existing setup.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Wait, really? What about pictures? Can I see them in the terminal?
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: You can. The CLI and TUI now draw images right in the chat instead of printing a file path.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Real pixels in the terminal. Finally.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: It works with full resolution in VS Code’s terminal if image support is on, and uses colored blocks elsewhere.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Right, back to the docs. You can also rewind a conversation now by pressing Esc twice or typing the command to fork from an earlier point.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Does the original session get deleted?
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: No, the original stays exactly as it was while you edit and resend the fork.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Nice. What about multiple machines? Do I have to switch windows?
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Desktop keeps all your gateways connected at once so switching between local and remote SSH instances is instant.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: The release notes say one-shot runs send about 1,570 fewer prompt tokens, and patch operations are faster with LSP on.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Fewer tokens per run. Efficient.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: And long-lived gateways let go of closed sessions' memory, so the sidebar doesn’t slow down even with 35,000 cron runs.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: From 121 seconds to instant? That’s a big jump.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Plugins also got an overhaul. You can update everything at once, and the catalog grew from about 600 to over 1,050 entries.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Is there a tier for vendor-built plugins?
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Yes, a new Verified tier marks plugins built by the vendor itself, and breaking updates are held back.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Please stay calm, we have more highlights. Paid tools now show price tags and spend limits in the approval prompt.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Does it stop me from overspending?
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: It asks before a chat goes over its limit, even in YOLO mode.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Group Chats run themselves now, with bots picking answers automatically and showing live status like 'scout · terminal · 7s'.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: And the skills are leaner, merged office skills into one, and you can lock them so the agent doesn’t rewrite them.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

claims.line: Correct. Five new official plugins including Meshy and ElevenLabs, and a keychain vault key for passwords.
claims.title: release:v0.23.0#highlights@v0.23.0:87a34c88

items.title: You run a permissions audit. It comes back clean. Nobody on the tenant team has permission to read the DNS credentials. The secret sits in the platform namespace, they cannot open it, and they have no access to the ClusterIssuer either.

claims.line: You run a permissions audit. It comes back clean. Nobody on the tenant team has permission to read the DNS credentials. The secret sits in the platform namespace, they cannot open it, and they have no access to the ClusterIssuer either.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: And somebody in that namespace can still make the controller spend those credentials.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Just by asking for them to be used.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: This part is about a boundary drawn around the wrong thing. Around who can read the key, instead of around who gets to decide where the key goes.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Start with what a Challenge is supposed to be. You ask cert-manager for a certificate. It creates an Order. The Order chooses a solver from the Issuer, and the solver is the policy: which DNS provider, which zones, which names it is allowed to answer for. Only then does the Order create a Challenge, which is the proof that you control the name.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: So in the intended flow, the solver has already been chosen by the time a Challenge exists. The Challenge carries the choice. It does not make it.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Now create one directly. A Challenge is an object in the tenant's namespace, and this tenant has been given permission to create it. Think about how little you need to hold to do it: create permission in one namespace, and nothing else. You never touch the secret, and you never read the ClusterIssuer. On create, cert-manager performs no admission validation tying it to an Order, to an owner, or to a solver the Issuer selected.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: So the object arrives with its own solver inside it. The controller picks it up and uses the solver the tenant wrote. The zone selector, the name selector, the labels, all the policy that was meant to fence the solver in, are never consulted, because they are consulted when the solver is chosen from the Issuer, and this object skipped that step.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Here is the turn. When the Challenge references a ClusterIssuer, cert-manager still takes two things from the ClusterIssuer: the namespace the DNS secret lives in, and whether ambient credentials are allowed. But it takes the provider configuration from the tenant's object. Platform credentials, tenant-chosen destination.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: With acme-dns, that is disclosure. The host named in the tenant's solver receives the API user and the API key that cert-manager loaded from the ClusterIssuer's namespace. The tenant never reads the secret. The controller reads it and hands it over.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: For other providers the advisory is careful, and so am I: credential use, policy bypass, and the risk of DNS changes on names the policy meant to exclude. It does not claim disclosure there without somebody demonstrating it provider by provider.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Ambient credentials. The key nobody typed, scoped to a cluster, available to a controller. That is the cloud conspiracy with a receipt: the credential you never see is the one that gets spent.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: You cannot blame the cloud for a controller that trusts a field. That is a code path, not a weather system.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Both are true. The credential sits there ambient, and the controller made it spendable by a tenant.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Then let me play the sceptic, because somebody has to. A namespace can create an object that a cluster-scoped controller acts on. Is that a flaw in cert-manager, or is that simply how RBAC works? What makes it a CVE?
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: The advisory answers that directly, and the answer holds. The documented workflow never asks a user to create a Challenge. A user asks for a certificate; cert-manager makes the Order, chooses the solver, makes the Challenge. So the create permission is not a security boundary. It arrived in the aggregate edit role.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Then take it out of the role.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Yes. And also stop the controller treating a hand-written solver as authoritative when the credential came from somewhere else. The advisory wants both, and it is right to. Reject standalone Challenges that no Order owns, and move Challenge and Order creation out of edit unless direct use is a boundary you genuinely support.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Fine. I withdraw it. It is RBAC plus a controller that believed a field it had no business knowing.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: That is the worst take of the week, by the way. Just RBAC, for a bug where the tenant never touches the secret and the controller does the rest.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: I will take it. It was a bad take and I enjoyed it.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: The part I would hate is being the person who reviewed that role and called it least privilege.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: Who does this reach? Multi-tenant clusters. You need a namespace user who can create Challenges, a controller reconciling them across the whole cluster, and a ClusterIssuer with a DNS solver whose secret sits in the cluster resource namespace, or which relies on ambient credentials. The aggregate edit role is enough to get a tenant there, which is the part that should make you go and look.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: And who does it not reach? If you are the only tenant, and everyone who can create objects in the cluster already holds the DNS credentials, there is no boundary to cross. That is not a defence. It is a smaller blast radius.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: The advisory went out on 29 October, and the fix is the patched release on both affected lines. Taking it costs a controller upgrade, and I would expect that to wait for a maintenance window, because so much depends on certificates being issued.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: And if you cannot take it tonight, you have a lever rather than a fix. Take Challenge and Order creation out of the aggregate edit role. The advisory lists that as a mitigation. It narrows the path. It does not close it, because the controller will still reconcile a direct object from anyone who holds the permission for some other reason.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: So the order is: upgrade, then find out who can create a Challenge and an Order in your cluster, then ask why that permission was ever in a role you hand to tenants.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: What does it teach?
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: That a credential is only as scoped as the object that decides where it goes. You can lock a secret in a namespace and still let a tenant point the machine that holds it at their own server.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: The boundary has to sit on the object the controller acts on. Not on the field the user fills in, and not on the read permission for the secret.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258

claims.line: The audit was clean. The audit was also answering a question nobody needed answered.
claims.title: GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258
